module_title: Method 10: Adaptive Reuse and Structural Retrofitting

lessons.title: Assessing a Building for Adaptive Reuse
lessons.body:
Before you spend money on a new use for an old building, you must assess it properly. Start with a walk-through. Look for cracks wider than 3 mm in walls, sagging roofs, and soft spots in floors. Use a 2 m straight edge and a spirit level to check for slopes. A floor that slopes more than 1 in 100 may need structural work. Check the foundation by digging small test pits around the base. Look for exposed footings, crumbling mortar, or roots pushing in. In many African towns, old buildings are made of mud brick, stone, or burnt brick with lime mortar. These are repairable, but you must use compatible materials.

Next, assess the walls. Tap them with a hammer. A hollow sound means the plaster has separated. Probe with a screwdriver. If it goes in easily, the material is rotten. Measure wall thickness. A 300 mm thick wall is usually load-bearing. Check for water damage: stains, mould, or efflorescence (white powder). Water is the biggest enemy. Look at the roof. Are rafters sagging? Are there leaks? A new roof may cost 20-30% of your total budget.

Check services. Old wiring may be cloth-insulated and dangerous. Plumbing may be lead or galvanised steel. You will likely need to rewire and re-pipe. Estimate costs: rewiring a 100 mÂ² building can cost $1,500-$3,000. Re-plumbing can cost $1,000-$2,500. Add 15% contingency. Also check legal status: is the building listed or in a heritage zone? In many African countries, you need permission from a heritage authority before making changes. Get this early.

Finally, decide if the building suits your new use. A warehouse with high ceilings and few windows is good for a craft market or workshop. A small house with many rooms is better for offices or a clinic. Draw a simple floor plan. Mark load-bearing walls, columns, and beams. Do not remove these without an engineer. If the building is more than 50% deteriorated, demolition and rebuild may be cheaper. But if the structure is sound, adaptive reuse saves 20-40% compared to new build, and keeps history alive.

lessons.title: Reinforcing Walls and Foundations
lessons.body:
Old walls often need reinforcement, especially if you add floors or heavy equipment. First, identify the weak points. Cracks that run diagonally from corners indicate settlement. Horizontal cracks in the middle of a wall suggest bulging. Use a crack gauge (a simple plastic ruler) to monitor movement. If cracks widen over a month, you have active movement. Stop and fix the foundation first.

For foundations, you can widen the existing footing. Dig alongside the wall, expose the old footing, and pour a new concrete strip 200 mm wider on each side. Use concrete with 1 part cement, 2 parts sand, 3 parts gravel (1:2:3). Add steel rebar 12 mm diameter, tied to the old footing with epoxy anchors. This spreads the load. For mud-brick walls, you can also inject a lime-based grout into cracks. Mix 1 part hydraulic lime, 3 parts fine sand, and water to a thin slurry. Pump it in with a grout pump or a large syringe. This fills voids and re-bonds the wall.

For wall reinforcement, use steel mesh and render. Fix galvanised welded mesh (50 mm x 50 mm) to the wall with nails or screws, then apply a 20 mm thick lime render. This adds tensile strength. For corners, use stainless steel helical bars (6 mm diameter) embedded in slots cut into the masonry. Fill the slots with lime mortar. This is called 'crack stitching'. It costs about $10 per metre but prevents cracks from reopening.

If you need to add a ring beam, pour a reinforced concrete beam on top of the walls. This ties the building together. Use 4 bars of 12 mm rebar and 6 mm stirrups at 200 mm centres. The beam should be at least 200 mm x 200 mm. For a small building, this can be done in sections to avoid shoring. Always support the roof temporarily with Acrow props before cutting into walls. Work in 1 m sections, and never remove more than 1 m of wall at a time. After reinforcement, monitor for 3 months. If no new cracks appear, you can proceed with the new use.

lessons.title: Adding New Elements Without Damaging Historic Fabric
lessons.body:
Historic fabric is the original material of the building: old bricks, timber beams, stone walls, and decorative tiles. Once damaged, it cannot be replaced. So when you add new elementsâstairs, mezzanines, toilets, or kitchensâyou must separate them from the old structure. The rule is: new work should be reversible and visually distinct. Do not chase new pipes into historic walls. Instead, run them in surface-mounted conduits or in a new service zone.

For a new mezzanine, use independent steel columns and beams. Do not bear them on old walls unless an engineer confirms the wall can take the load. A typical mezzanine for a craft market might be 50 mÂ² and carry 300 kg/mÂ². Use 150 mm x 150 mm steel columns, 200 mm x 100 mm beams, and 50 mm timber decking. Anchor the columns to a new concrete pad, not to the old floor. This way, if the mezzanine is removed later, the historic floor is untouched.

For new openings, avoid cutting through decorative features. If you must cut a door in a historic wall, use a diamond blade saw and stitch the edges with lime mortar. Never use a sledgehammer. Support the wall above with Acrow props and a strong boy (a horizontal beam). Cut in small sections. After cutting, line the opening with a stainless steel frame or a timber lintel treated with preservative. For windows, keep the original frames if possible. Repair with linseed oil putty and replace broken glass with hand-blown or recycled glass to match.

For new toilets, build a separate block or use a corner that is not original. Use a raised floor with a waterproof membrane. Connect drains to a new septic tank or sewer line, not to old drains. If you must run a pipe through a historic wall, drill a hole 50 mm larger than the pipe, wrap the pipe in foam, and seal with flexible mastic. This allows movement without cracking the wall. Always photograph and document every change. In many African heritage sites, you need approval for any alteration. Keep a log of materials and methods.

lessons.title: Converting Old Buildings for New Business Uses
lessons.body:
Old buildings can become shops, restaurants, offices, or workshops. But you must match the building to the business. A restaurant needs water, drainage, and ventilation. An office needs power, internet, and daylight. A workshop needs heavy power and a strong floor. Start by listing your needs. Then check the building against them. If the building has no water supply, you can add a tank and pump, but that costs $500-$1,500. If it has no three-phase power, you may need a new connection from the utility, which can cost $2,000 or more.

For a shop or restaurant, you need a visible entrance and good frontage. If the old building has small windows, you can enlarge them, but only with engineer approval. For a craft market, you need open space and stalls. Use the existing columns and beams to define stall areas. Each stall should be at least 2 m x 2 m. Provide a central aisle of 3 m for customers. Add a new roof over the central area if the old roof leaks. Use corrugated metal sheets with insulation to reduce heat. In hot climates, add a ridge vent to let hot air escape.

For offices, you need partitions. Build them as free-standing units that do not touch the historic ceiling. Use 100 mm metal studs with plasterboard. This is cheap and easy to remove. For a clinic, you need cleanable surfaces. Use ceramic tiles on floors and washable paint on walls. But do not cover historic tiles or plaster. Instead, lay new tiles on a separating membrane.

Budget carefully. A typical conversion of a 200 mÂ² old building might cost: structural repairs $10,000; new roof $8,000; electrical $5,000; plumbing $4,000; partitions and finishes $7,000. Total $34,000. That is $170/mÂ², which is often 30% less than new build. But add 20% contingency. Also check zoning laws: can you run a business in a residential area? In many African cities, you need a change of use permit. Get it before you start. Finally, involve the local community. They can help with labour and support your business.

lessons.title: Energy Efficiency Upgrades for Old Buildings
lessons.body:
Old buildings are often leaky and dark, but you can make them energy efficient without destroying their character. Start with the roof. In hot climates, the roof is the biggest source of heat. If you have a metal roof, add a radiant barrier: a layer of aluminium foil facing down. This reflects heat. Or add 50 mm of polyurethane insulation board under the roof sheets. This can reduce indoor temperature by 5-10Â°C. For thatched roofs, keep them thick (at least 200 mm) and repair gaps. Thatched roofs are naturally insulating.

Next, tackle windows. Old windows are often single-glazed and draughty. Do not replace them with modern uPVC if the building is historic. Instead, add secondary glazing: a second pane of glass on the inside, fixed with a timber frame. This creates an air gap and reduces heat loss or gain by 50%. Use low-e glass if you can afford it. For ventilation, keep original openings but add insect screens. In hot climates, you want cross-ventilation. Open windows on opposite sides. If you need air conditioning, use inverter split units (1.5 kW for a 20 mÂ² room). Set the thermostat to 24Â°C. This uses 30% less power than non-inverter units.

Lighting is easy. Replace all bulbs with LED. A 9 W LED gives the same light as a 60 W incandescent. For a 200 mÂ² building, you might have 50 bulbs. Switching to LED saves 50 x 51 W = 2,550 W. If used 6 hours a day, that saves 15 kWh per day, or 450 kWh per month. At $0.15/kWh, that is $67 saved per month. Payback in 3 months.

For water heating, use solar. A 150 L solar water heater costs $500-$800 and saves 2,000 kWh per year. That is $300 per year. Also, insulate hot water pipes with foam lagging. For walls, if they are solid and cold, you can add internal insulation, but this reduces room size. Use 25 mm aerogel or 50 mm wood fibre board. Always leave a breather membrane to avoid trapping moisture. Finally, use ceiling fans instead of AC where possible. A 75 W fan can make a room feel 4Â°C cooler. In many African cities, fans are enough for most of the year.

lessons.title: Case Study: Turning an Old Warehouse into a Craft Market
lessons.body:
In 2019, a group in Accra, Ghana, converted a 1950s warehouse into a craft market. The warehouse was 500 mÂ², with a steel truss roof, brick walls, and a concrete floor. It had been empty for 10 years. The roof leaked, and one wall had a 5 m long diagonal crack. The group had a budget of $50,000. They started with an assessment. An engineer found the crack was caused by a blocked drain that had softened the foundation. They fixed the drain and widened the footing with a concrete strip, costing $3,000. They stitched the crack with helical bars and lime mortar, costing $800.

Next, they repaired the roof. They replaced 30% of the corrugated sheets, added a radiant barrier, and installed 5 skylights (1 m x 1 m) to bring in daylight. Cost: $8,000. They kept the original steel trusses, wire-brushed them, and painted with red oxide primer. For the walls, they repointed the mortar with lime and sand (1:3). They did not render over the bricks, leaving them exposed for character. They added a new concrete floor in one corner for a cafÃ©, using a separating membrane. Cost: $2,500.

For the market, they built 20 stalls, each 2 m x 2 m, using free-standing steel frames and timber counters. These were placed along the walls and in two rows in the centre, with 3 m aisles. Cost: $6,000. They added a new toilet block outside, with a septic tank and soakaway. Cost: $7,000. Electrical work included new wiring, LED lights, and 10 sockets for vendors. Cost: $4,000. Plumbing for the cafÃ© and toilets cost $3,000.

They also added a solar water heater for the cafÃ© and 10 solar panels (3 kW) to reduce grid dependence. Cost: $5,000. The total spent was $39,300, leaving a contingency. The market opened in 2020 with 20 vendors. Rent is $50 per stall per month, generating $1,000 per month. The building now serves the community and preserves a piece of industrial heritage. Key lessons: fix water problems first, keep original materials, use free-standing new elements, and involve vendors in design.

quiz.q: What is the first thing you should look for when assessing a building for adaptive reuse?
options: A) The colour of the paint
D) The age of the roof
quiz.explanation: Cracks wider than 3 mm indicate structural movement that must be addressed before reuse.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to check for slopes in floors?
quiz.explanation: A spirit level and straight edge are used to measure slopes and levelness.

quiz.q: What does a hollow sound when tapping a wall indicate?
quiz.explanation: A hollow sound means the plaster has debonded from the wall.

quiz.q: What is the biggest enemy of old buildings?
quiz.explanation: Water causes rot, erosion, and foundation movement, leading to major damage.

quiz.q: What percentage of your budget might a new roof cost?
quiz.explanation: A new roof often costs 20-30% of the total conversion budget.

quiz.q: Why should you get heritage approval early?
options: A) To avoid fines and stop-work orders
quiz.explanation: Unauthorized changes to heritage buildings can lead to fines and legal stops.

quiz.q: What is the first step in reinforcing a foundation?
options: B) Dig alongside and expose the old footing
quiz.explanation: You must expose the existing footing to widen it effectively.

quiz.q: What concrete mix is recommended for a new footing?
quiz.explanation: A 1:2:3 mix (cement:sand:gravel) is standard for structural concrete.

quiz.q: What is crack stitching?
options: B) Embedding helical bars in slots
quiz.explanation: Crack stitching uses stainless steel helical bars in lime mortar to tie cracks together.

quiz.q: How long should you monitor after reinforcement before proceeding?
quiz.explanation: Three months of monitoring ensures no new movement occurs.

quiz.q: What is 'historic fabric'?
options: B) Original materials of the building
quiz.explanation: Historic fabric refers to the original building materials and features.

quiz.q: When adding a mezzanine, where should columns be anchored?
options: B) To a new concrete pad
quiz.explanation: New columns should be independent, anchored to new foundations, not historic walls.

quiz.q: What tool should you use to cut a new opening in a historic wall?
quiz.explanation: A diamond blade saw makes clean cuts with less vibration and damage.

quiz.q: How should new pipes be run through historic walls?
options: B) Surface-mounted or in a sleeve
quiz.explanation: Surface mounting or using a sleeve allows movement and avoids damaging historic fabric.

quiz.q: Why should new elements be reversible?
options: A) To allow future removal without damage
quiz.explanation: Reversible additions can be removed later, preserving the historic building.

quiz.q: What is a key need for a restaurant conversion?
quiz.explanation: Restaurants require significant water supply and drainage for kitchens and toilets.

quiz.q: How wide should a central aisle be in a craft market?
quiz.explanation: A 3 m aisle allows comfortable movement for customers and vendors.

quiz.q: What is a cost-effective partition for offices in an old building?
quiz.explanation: Metal stud partitions are lightweight, cheap, and easy to remove.

quiz.q: What permit may be needed to run a business in a residential area?
quiz.explanation: A change of use permit is required to legally operate a business in a residential zone.

quiz.q: What is a typical cost per square metre for converting an old building?
quiz.explanation: The case study showed about $170/mÂ², often 30% less than new build.

quiz.q: What is a radiant barrier used for?
quiz.explanation: A radiant barrier reflects heat away from the building, reducing cooling loads.

quiz.q: How much can secondary glazing reduce heat gain or loss?
quiz.explanation: Secondary glazing creates an air gap that cuts heat transfer by about 50%.

quiz.q: What is the power saving of a 9 W LED compared to a 60 W incandescent?
quiz.explanation: A 9 W LED replaces a 60 W bulb, saving 51 W per bulb.

quiz.q: What is the payback period for LED lighting in the example?
quiz.explanation: The monthly savings of $67 recoup the cost in about 3 months.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of ceiling fans over air conditioning?
quiz.explanation: Fans use much less electricity than AC and can make a room feel 4Â°C cooler.

quiz.q: In the case study, what caused the diagonal crack in the warehouse wall?
options: B) Blocked drain softening the foundation
quiz.explanation: A blocked drain led to water softening the foundation, causing settlement.

quiz.q: How much did the case study spend on fixing the foundation?
quiz.explanation: Widening the footing and fixing the drain cost $3,000.

quiz.q: What did the case study use for the cafÃ© floor?
options: B) New concrete on a separating membrane
D) Tiles directly on old floor
quiz.explanation: A separating membrane allows the new floor to be removed without damaging the historic floor.

quiz.q: How many stalls were built in the case study?
quiz.explanation: They built 20 stalls, each 2 m x 2 m.

quiz.q: What was the total cost of the case study conversion?
quiz.explanation: The total spent was $39,300, within the $50,000 budget.
